name: Aloo Paratha with Curd (North Indian)
description: Whole wheat flatbread stuffed with a spiced mashed potato filling, pan-fried until golden and flaky, served with a cooling side of plain curd (yoghurt).

items.name: whole wheat flour (atta), plus extra for dusting
Water, as needed to knead (add gradually, roughly 2 tbsp at a time, until a soft, pliable dough forms)
cumin seeds (or ½ tsp roasted cumin powder)
dried mango powder (amchur) or 1 tsp lemon juice
ghee or oil (roughly ½ tbsp per paratha)
plain curd (yoghurt), i.e. about 4 tbsp per person

steps: Making the dough

Knead: In a large bowl, combine the flour and salt. Add the oil and rub it in lightly. Gradually add water, mixing and kneading until a soft, smooth dough forms (it should be slightly softer than roti dough, as this makes rolling stuffed parathas easier).
Rest: Cover the dough with a damp cloth and let it rest for at least 15 minutes.
Making the filling

Combine: In a separate bowl, mix the mashed potato with coriander, green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds, red chilli powder, turmeric (if using), garam masala, amchur or lemon juice, and salt. Mix well, mashing any large lumps so the filling is smooth enough to stuff easily — but don't add any water, it should stay dry and crumbly-soft.
Portion: Divide the filling into 8 equal portions and roll each into a smooth ball.
Assembling and rolling
Divide the dough: Divide the rested dough into 8 equal portions and roll into smooth balls.

Stuff: Take one dough ball, dust with a little flour, and roll it out into a small disc about the width of your palm. Place one portion of the potato filling in the centre. Bring the edges of the dough up and over the filling, pinching them together at the top to seal completely, then gently flatten into a ball again.

Roll out: Dust with flour and gently roll the stuffed ball into a flat, round paratha about the size of a small side plate — roll evenly and gently to avoid the filling bursting through. Don't worry if a little filling peeks out; that's normal.
Cooking
Heat the pan: Heat a flat griddle (tawa) on medium heat.
Cook the first side: Place the rolled paratha on the hot griddle. Cook for about 1 minute, until small bubbles start to appear on the surface.
Flip and add fat: Flip it over, spread about ½ tsp of ghee or oil over the top, and cook for another minute.

Flip again and finish: Flip once more, spread ½ tsp of ghee or oil on the other side too, and press gently with a spatula all over the surface. Cook, flipping once or twice more, until both sides are golden brown with crisp, slightly charred spots (about 3–4 minutes total).
Repeat: Remove and keep warm, wrapped in a clean cloth. Repeat with the remaining dough and filling portions.
Serving
Serve hot: Serve each paratha with a generous side of plain curd, and pickle or a dollop of butter if desired.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 2 parathas with curd per serving.
egg_check_notes: This recipe is naturally egg-free — atta, potatoes, spices, ghee, and curd contain no eggs. The only thing worth double-checking is if you ever buy ready-made atta blends or "instant paratha" mixes, as some multigrain or "enriched" varieties occasionally include additives — always check the pack, though plain wholemeal atta from an Indian grocer or the Tesco/Sainsbury's world foods aisle is reliably egg-free.
common_mistakes: Overfilling the paratha or rolling too aggressively causes the filling to burst through — roll gently and evenly, applying light pressure. Not resting the dough leads to parathas that shrink back and are harder to roll thin. Skipping the ghee/oil on both sides during cooking results in a drier, less flaky paratha.
uk_sourcing_notes: Whole wheat atta (often labelled "chapati flour") is widely available at Indian grocers and in the world foods aisle of larger UK supermarkets. Amchur (dried mango powder) is a specialty item best found at an Indian grocer — lemon juice is a fine substitute if unavailable.
storage_notes: The potato filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated. Rolled, uncooked parathas can be layered with baking paper between them and frozen for up to a month — cook from frozen, adding an extra minute or two per side. Cooked parathas keep in the fridge for 2 days; reheat on a dry tawa or in a pan, not the microwave, to keep them from turning rubbery.

name: Baingan Bharta with Bajra Roti
description: Smoky, fire-roasted mashed aubergine cooked down with onions, tomatoes, and spices, paired with a rustic, hand-patted pearl millet flatbread.

items.name: oil (mustard oil is traditional, but any vegetable oil works)
bajra flour (pearl millet flour), plus extra for dusting
Hot (just-boiled) water, as needed to bind

steps: 8. Bind the dough: In a bowl, combine the bajra flour and salt. Gradually pour in hot water, mixing first with a spoon (it's too hot to knead by hand at this stage), then knead into a soft dough once cool enough to handle — bajra has no gluten, so work it while still slightly warm for the best texture.
9. Divide: Divide the dough into 6–8 balls.

10. Pat out: Pat or gently roll each ball between two sheets of cling film (or on a floured surface) into a roti about ¼ inch thick. It may crack at the edges — this is normal; just patch with your fingers.

11. Cook: Cook on a hot, dry tawa on medium heat with no oil. Flip once bubbles appear, then cook both sides, pressing gently with a folded cloth, until light brown spots form, about 2–3 minutes per side.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on bharta with 2 bajra roti per serving.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free.
common_mistakes: Under-charring the aubergine loses the signature smoky flavour — don't rush this step. Rolling the bajra dough once it's gone cold makes it crack apart — pat it out while still slightly warm.
uk_sourcing_notes: Aubergine is in every UK supermarket. Bajra flour (sometimes labelled "pearl millet flour") is available at Indian grocers and some larger world foods aisles.
storage_notes: Bharta keeps 2 days refrigerated and tastes even better the next day. Bajra roti is best eaten fresh — the dough doesn't keep well, so make it the same day.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the green chillies and reduce the red chilli powder for a milder version.

name: Basundi
description: A rich, slow-simmered sweetened milk dessert flavoured with saffron and cardamom, thickened naturally by reduction — a traditional festive treat, similar to rabri but thinner and pourable.

steps: Simmer the milk: Pour the milk into a heavy-bottomed, wide pan and bring to a gentle boil on medium heat. Once boiling, reduce the heat to low-medium and let it simmer, stirring frequently and scraping down the sides, for about 35–40 minutes, until it reduces to roughly half its original volume and thickens slightly.

Prevent sticking: Continue scraping the cream (malai) that forms on the sides back into the milk periodically — this is what gives basundi its characteristic rich texture, so don't skip it, but be gentle to avoid scorching the bottom.
Sweeten: Once thickened to a pourable, creamy consistency, stir in the sugar and cook for another 5 minutes until fully dissolved.
Flavour: Add the saffron-soaked milk and cardamom powder, and stir well to combine.
Add nuts: Stir in the chopped pistachios, almonds, and cashews (if using), reserving a little for garnish.
Cool and chill: Remove from heat and let it cool to room temperature (it will thicken further as it cools), then refrigerate for at least 2 hours.
Serve: Serve chilled, garnished with the reserved chopped nuts.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — milk, sugar, and nuts carry no hidden egg risk.
common_mistakes: Using medium-high heat to rush the reduction is the most common mistake — it causes scorching on the bottom, which taints the whole batch with a burnt flavour. Low and slow, with frequent stirring, is essential. Also, adding sugar too early can slow down the reduction process, so add it once the milk has already thickened.
uk_sourcing_notes: Use whole/full-fat milk from any UK supermarket for the best richness — semi-skimmed will work but gives a noticeably lighter result. Saffron, pistachios, and cardamom are all at any Indian grocer.
storage_notes: Basundi keeps well refrigerated for 3–4 days in an airtight container, and the flavour actually improves after a day. Not suitable for freezing, as the texture separates.
kid_friendly_notes: No heat in this dish — naturally kid-friendly. Reduce sugar slightly if serving to very young children, as it's traditionally quite sweet.

name: Bhel Puri
description: A crunchy, tangy-sweet puffed rice snack tossed with vegetables, tamarind and mint chutneys, and crispy sev — a classic Mumbai beach-side favourite.

items.name: sev (thin gram flour noodles — check label, see egg-check note)
–8 puri (small round crisp puris — check label, see egg-check note), crushed roughly

steps: Make the tamarind chutney: Combine the tamarind pulp, jaggery, red chilli powder, cumin powder, salt, and water in a small pan. Simmer on low heat for 5–6 minutes until slightly thickened and glossy. Cool before using.
Make the mint chutney: Blend the mint, coriander, green chilli, lemon juice, salt, and water into a smooth, bright green paste.
Combine the base: In a large bowl, mix the puffed rice, chopped onion, tomato, and boiled potato.
Add chutneys: Add 3–4 tbsp of tamarind chutney and 2–3 tbsp of mint chutney (adjust to taste). Toss well and quickly — bhel goes soggy fast once mixed.
Add crunch: Add the crushed puris, sev, chaat masala, and lemon juice. Toss everything together lightly.
Serve immediately: Garnish with coriander and extra sev on top. Serve at once — bhel must be eaten right after mixing to stay crisp.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
common_mistakes: Mixing the bhel too far ahead of eating is the single biggest mistake — the puffed rice turns soggy within minutes. Prep all components ahead, but only toss together just before serving.
uk_sourcing_notes: Puffed rice, sev, and small puris are sold at any Indian grocer, usually in the snacks/namkeen aisle. Tamarind pulp/concentrate is also widely available there or in larger supermarket world foods aisles.
storage_notes: Both chutneys keep well refrigerated for up to a week. All dry components (puffed rice, sev, puris) can be prepped ahead, but only combine everything right before serving.
kid_friendly_notes: Reduce or omit the green chilli in the mint chutney and go lighter on chaat masala for a milder, kid-friendly version — the tamarind chutney's sweetness usually appeals to kids regardless.

name: Bhindi Masala with Phulka
description: Okra stir-fried until lightly crisp with onions, tomatoes, and warming spices, served with soft, puffed whole wheat flatbreads.

items.name: okra (bhindi), washed, thoroughly dried, trimmed and sliced into rounds or lengthways
amchur (dried mango powder), optional, for tang
whole wheat flour (atta), plus extra for dusting

steps: 7. Knead: Combine the flour and salt, then gradually add water, kneading into a smooth, soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.
8. Roll: Divide into 8 balls. Roll each into a thin, even round on a lightly floured surface.
9. Cook: Place on a hot tawa. Cook briefly until small bubbles appear, then flip.

10. Puff: Cook the second side briefly, then transfer directly onto an open flame (or press firmly with a folded cloth on the tawa) — it should puff up like a balloon within seconds. Remove, smear lightly with ghee if desired, and keep wrapped in a cloth.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on bhindi masala with 2 phulka per serving.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — okra, spices, atta, and ghee carry no hidden egg risk.
common_mistakes: Not drying the okra thoroughly before cooking is the #1 cause of slimy bhindi. Overcrowding the pan while searing it causes steaming rather than browning — use a wide pan. Cooking phulka on too low a heat prevents it from puffing.
uk_sourcing_notes: Okra is sold as "okra" or "ladies' fingers" at most larger Tesco/Sainsbury's and any Indian or Caribbean grocer. Atta as usual from the world foods aisle or Indian grocer.
storage_notes: Bhindi masala keeps 1–2 days refrigerated, though the okra softens further. Phulka dough can be made ahead and refrigerated, but roll and cook fresh for best puffing.
kid_friendly_notes: Reduce the chilli powder and omit the amchur if a tangier note isn't preferred.

name: Dahi Puri
description: Crisp hollow puris filled with spiced potato, topped with cooling yoghurt, tangy-sweet chutneys, and crunchy sev — a favourite creamy variation on Mumbai chaat.

steps: Make the tamarind chutney: Simmer tamarind pulp, jaggery, chilli powder, cumin powder, salt, and water for 5–6 minutes until slightly thickened. Cool.
Make the mint chutney: Blend mint, coriander, green chilli, lemon juice, salt, and water into a smooth paste.
Prep the yoghurt: Whisk the yoghurt with a pinch of salt and sugar until smooth and slightly loosened (add a splash of water if it's very thick — it should be pourable but still creamy).
Fill the puris: Gently tap a small hole into the top of each hollow puri (or use the pre-made opening) and fill each with a little diced potato and a few chickpeas or sprouts, if using.
Top with yoghurt: Spoon a little whisked yoghurt over the filling in each puri.
Add chutneys: Drizzle a little tamarind chutney and mint chutney over each.
Finish: Sprinkle chaat masala, roasted cumin powder, and a touch of red chilli powder over the top. Scatter with sev and coriander leaves.
Serve immediately: Dahi puri must be eaten right away — the puris will turn soggy quickly once filled.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 6 puris per serving.
common_mistakes: Overfilling the puris makes them prone to breaking apart — a small amount of filling goes a long way. Using thin, watery yoghurt makes the dish messy — it should be thick enough to hold its place on top of the filling.
uk_sourcing_notes: Hollow puris (sometimes labelled "golgappa" or "puri for pani puri") and sev are sold at any Indian grocer. Thick yoghurt — Greek-style plain yoghurt from any UK supermarket works very well here.
storage_notes: Both chutneys and the whisked yoghurt keep for a couple of days refrigerated. Assemble the puris only right before serving.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the green chilli from the mint chutney and skip the chilli powder garnish — the yoghurt naturally mellows the dish, so kids often enjoy it as is.

name: Dal Fry with Jeera Rice
description: Comforting split-pigeon-pea dal finished with a garlicky cumin tempering, served alongside fragrant cumin-flavoured rice.

items.name: Water, as needed for boiling (enough to cover dal by about 2 inches)
–3 cloves and 1-inch cinnamon stick (optional whole spices)
Water, as needed to cook the rice (roughly double the volume of rice)

steps: Boil the dal: In a pot, combine the rinsed dal, turmeric, salt, and enough water to cover by about 2 inches. Boil until soft and mushy, about 20–25 minutes (or 3–4 whistles in a pressure cooker). Mash lightly with a spoon or whisk, adding hot water if it's too thick.
Make the tempering: Heat the ghee in a small pan on medium heat. Add cumin and mustard seeds and let them sizzle.
Add aromatics: Add the garlic, dried red chilli, and hing, and sauté for 30 seconds.
Cook onion and tomato: Add the onion and cook until golden, about 4 minutes. Add the tomato and chilli powder, cooking until soft and the oil separates, about 5 minutes.
Combine: Pour the tempering into the boiled dal, mix well, and simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in the garam masala and fresh coriander.
6. Rinse: Wash the rice until the water runs mostly clear; soak for 15 minutes if you have time.
7. Temper: Heat the ghee in a pot on medium heat. Add cumin seeds and whole spices, letting them sizzle.
8. Add rice: Add the drained rice and sauté gently for 1–2 minutes to coat it in the ghee.

9. Cook: Add water and salt, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low heat for 12–15 minutes until the rice is cooked and the water is absorbed. Rest, covered, off the heat for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: Naturally egg-free. Ready-made Malvani masala pastes/powders are traditionally a dry spice blend with no egg, but glance at the label as a precaution with any pre-made paste product.
common_mistakes: Letting the masala paste burn in step 4 (it needs constant stirring — add a splash of water if it sticks). Not patting the bhakri thin and even enough leaves the centre undercooked.
uk_sourcing_notes: Ready-made Malvani masala paste or powder can be found at larger Indian grocers; if your local grocer doesn't stock a Maharashtrian-specific brand, Indian grocery specialists online usually do. Rice flour is available at any Indian grocer or in the baking aisle of larger supermarkets.
storage_notes: The curry keeps 2 days refrigerated and improves in flavour overnight. Bhakri is best fresh — it hardens once cooled and doesn't store well.
kid_friendly_notes: Malvani masala is quite pungent and spicy — reduce the quantity significantly for children, or stir in a little extra coconut to mellow the heat.

name: Chilli Paneer with Fried Rice
description: Crispy fried paneer tossed in a tangy, garlicky chilli-soy sauce, served alongside a smoky vegetable fried rice — a beloved Indo-Chinese restaurant classic, made at home.

items.name: –3 tbsp water, as needed to make a thick coating batter
Oil, for shallow or deep frying
green pepper, cut into chunky squares
soy sauce (check label — see egg-check note)
red chilli sauce (or sriracha, adjust to taste)
cornflour, mixed with 2 tbsp water (for thickening)
onions, sliced (green and white parts separated), for garnish and cooking
rice (raw, uncooked measure — use long-grain or basmati; cook and cool before using)
finely chopped mixed vegetables (carrot, French beans, sweetcorn — diced small)
onions, sliced (white and green parts separated)
Salt, to taste (go easy, as soy sauce is already salty)

steps: Chilli Paneer

Make the batter: In a bowl, mix the cornflour, plain flour, ginger-garlic paste, black pepper, and salt. Gradually add water to form a thick, coating batter (not runny). Add the paneer cubes and toss gently to coat evenly. Let it sit for 15–20 minutes.

Fry the paneer: Heat oil in a pan (enough for shallow frying, about ½ inch deep). Fry the coated paneer cubes in batches for 3–4 minutes, turning occasionally, until golden and crisp on all sides. Drain on kitchen paper.
Prepare the sauce mix: In a small bowl, combine the soy sauce, ketchup, red chilli sauce, vinegar, and sugar with the 4 tbsp water. Set aside.
Start the stir-fry: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large pan or wok on high heat. Add the chopped garlic, ginger, and green chillies, and stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add vegetables: Add the onion petals, pepper squares, and the white parts of the spring onions. Stir-fry on high heat for 2–3 minutes, keeping the vegetables crunchy, not soft.
Add sauce: Pour in the prepared sauce mixture and bring to a bubble. Add the cornflour-water mixture and stir continuously for 1–2 minutes until the sauce thickens and turns glossy.

Toss in paneer: Add the fried paneer cubes and toss quickly to coat in the sauce, cooking for just 1 minute more so the paneer doesn't turn soggy. Garnish with the green parts of the spring onion. Set aside, keeping warm.
Vegetable Fried Rice

Cook the rice: If starting with raw rice, cook until just done, with grains separate (not mushy). Spread on a tray and cool completely — this is essential for good fried rice texture, so ideally cook this in advance or use leftover rice.
Start the stir-fry: Heat the oil in a large pan or wok on high heat. Add the chopped garlic and stir-fry for 20–30 seconds.
Add vegetables: Add the mixed diced vegetables and the white parts of the spring onions. Stir-fry on high heat for 2–3 minutes until just tender but still with a slight bite.
Add cabbage: Add the shredded cabbage and stir-fry for another minute.
Add rice: Add the cooled rice to the pan. Using a folding motion, toss it through the vegetables so the grains stay separate and don't get mushy.

Season: Add the soy sauce, vinegar, black pepper, and salt (if needed). Toss everything together on high heat for 2–3 minutes until well combined and evenly coated. Garnish with the green parts of the spring onion.
Serving
Serve: Plate the fried rice with the chilli paneer alongside, and serve immediately while both are hot.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
common_mistakes: Overcrowding the pan when frying paneer or stir-frying vegetables lowers the heat and causes steaming instead of a proper sear/crisp — cook in batches on high heat. Adding the cornflour-water slurry too early or without stirring constantly can cause lumps — add it in a thin stream while stirring. Using warm rice for fried rice leads to a mushy, clumped result — always cool it fully first, ideally use rice cooked a day ahead and refrigerated.
uk_sourcing_notes: Soy sauce, rice vinegar, and chilli sauce are all easily found in the world foods aisle of any UK supermarket. Ginger-garlic paste can be bought ready-made at Indian grocers, or made fresh by blending equal parts ginger and garlic.
storage_notes: The chilli sauce mixture (step 3) can be prepped ahead and refrigerated for up to 2 days. Cooked, cooled rice keeps well in the fridge for a day, ready for fried rice the next day. Both dishes are best eaten fresh, though leftovers reheat reasonably well in a hot pan (avoid microwaving the paneer, as it turns rubbery).
kid_friendly_notes: Reduce or omit the green chillies and red chilli sauce for a much milder version — a little extra ketchup can round out the flavour without adding heat.

name: Ghevar
description: A honeycomb-textured, deep-fried disc made from a thin batter, soaked in sugar syrup and topped with rabri (thickened sweet milk) and nuts — an intricate, festive Rajasthani sweet, traditionally made for Teej and Raksha Bandhan.

items.name: ghee, chilled and solid (or chilled butter)
Ice-cold water, as needed (roughly 20–24 tbsp, added gradually)
A few ice cubes, kept in the mixing bowl while beating the batter
A few drops of lemon juice
basundi or rabri (thickened sweetened milk — see Basundi recipe above for a homemade version, or use a good-quality shop-bought rabri)
A few strands of saffron, for garnish
Ghee or oil, enough for deep frying (about 2 inches deep in a narrow, deep pot)

steps: Making the batter
Rub in the ghee: In a large bowl, rub the chilled ghee into the flour with your fingertips until it resembles coarse breadcrumbs.

Add ice water: Gradually add ice-cold water, a little at a time, whisking continuously (a hand whisk or electric beater works well) until you get a very thin, smooth, pourable batter — similar to a thin pancake batter, with no lumps. Keep a few ice cubes in the bowl while you work to keep everything cold, which helps the layered texture form.
Rest: Let the batter rest in the fridge for at least 30 minutes.
Making the sugar syrup

Make one-string syrup: Combine the sugar and water in a small pan and bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Simmer for 5–6 minutes until it reaches a one-string consistency (a small drop between your fingers should form a single thin thread when pulled apart gently). Stir in the cardamom powder and lemon juice, and keep warm.
Frying the ghevar
Heat the oil/ghee: Heat the ghee or oil in a deep, narrow pot on medium heat until quite hot but not smoking.

Pour the batter: Using a ladle, pour a thin stream of batter into the centre of the hot oil from a small height, letting it spread and set for a few seconds before adding more in a circular motion, building up the honeycomb structure layer by layer. This takes patience and a steady hand — go slowly.

Fry: Continue building the disc for several minutes until it's about ½–¾ inch thick and holds together, with visible small holes throughout (the "honeycomb" look). Fry until golden and crisp, then carefully lift out with a skewer or slotted implement and drain on kitchen paper.
Repeat: Repeat with the remaining batter to make 4–5 discs, letting the oil return to temperature between each.
Finishing
Soak in syrup: While still warm, dip each ghevar disc briefly into the warm sugar syrup, then remove and let excess drip off.
Top: Spoon a generous layer of basundi or rabri over the top of each disc. Garnish with chopped pistachios, almonds, and a few saffron strands.
Serve: Best served fresh, at room temperature or lightly chilled.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 1 topped ghevar disc per serving.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — flour, ghee, sugar, and milk carry no hidden egg risk.
common_mistakes: Warm batter or warm ghee/oil temperature both prevent the signature honeycomb structure from forming — everything (batter, water, even the bowl) should stay as cold as possible until the moment of frying. Pouring the batter too quickly or in a thick stream results in a dense, solid disc rather than the airy, layered texture.
uk_sourcing_notes: All ingredients here (flour, ghee, sugar) are standard UK supermarket items. A ghevar mould isn't essential — a narrow, deep, straight-sided pot (like a small milk pan) works as a home substitute to help the disc hold its shape while frying.
storage_notes: Fried, un-soaked ghevar discs (without syrup or topping) keep well in an airtight container for about a week at room temperature. Soak in syrup and top with rabri only just before serving, as the topping softens the texture over time.
kid_friendly_notes: No heat in this dish — naturally kid-friendly, though it's quite rich and sweet, so smaller portions suit younger children well.

name: Kanda Poha (Maharashtrian Style)
description: A light, tangy breakfast of flattened rice sautéed with onions, peanuts, and a mustard-cumin tempering — soft yet fluffy, never mushy.

items.name: potato, finely diced (optional, but common in home-style versions)

steps: Rinse the poha: Place the poha in a sieve or colander and rinse briefly under running water — just 2–3 quick passes, do not soak or leave sitting in water. Drain fully and set aside for 5–10 minutes; it should soften and turn fluffy on its own. Fluff gently with your fingers, don't compress it.
Start the tempering: Heat the oil in a wide pan or kadhai on medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them splutter.
Add aromatics: Add the cumin seeds, hing, curry leaves, and green chillies. Sauté for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add peanuts: Add the peanuts and sauté for a minute until lightly golden and toasty.

Cook onion and potato: Add the chopped onion (and potato, if using). Cook on medium heat for 5–6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion turns soft and translucent and the potato is fork-tender.
Season: Add turmeric, sugar, and salt. Stir well so the oil turns a light yellow and everything is evenly coated.

Add the poha: Add the softened poha to the pan. Using a light hand (like folding, not stirring), toss it gently with the onion-potato mixture so it doesn't break or turn mushy. Cover and let it steam on low heat for 2–3 minutes.
Finish: Turn off the heat. Squeeze over the lemon juice, sprinkle with fresh coriander, and toss once more gently. Garnish with sev just before serving (it goes soggy if left sitting).

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: Every ingredient here — poha, peanuts, oil, spices, potato, onion — is naturally egg-free. The only ingredient to double-check is shop-bought sev: it's traditionally made from gram flour and egg-free, but always glance at the pack for allergen warnings, especially with mixed "namkeen" brands that sometimes share lines with other products. Common mistake: Soaking poha in water (rather than a quick rinse) is the #1 cause of mushy poha — it turns to paste once cooked. A brief rinse and rest is all it needs.
uk_sourcing_notes: Poha (flattened rice) and sev are both easily found at any Indian grocer, or in the "world foods" aisle of larger Tesco/Asda stores. Regular thin poha works too, but rinse it even more briefly (1 quick pass) as it softens faster than thick poha.
storage_notes: Best eaten fresh, but leftovers keep covered in the fridge for a day. Reheat in a pan with a small splash of water to loosen it back up — microwaving tends to dry it out. Spice level: Omit or deseed the green chillies for a kid-friendly version. Some families also add a few raisins or a spoon of grated coconut on top for a sweeter, milder finish.

name: Kothimbir Vadi
description: Steamed and pan-fried coriander and gram flour savoury bites, lightly spiced and crisped at the edges — a popular Maharashtrian tea-time snack.

ingredients.group: For the tempering (optional, for extra flavour after steaming)

steps: Make the batter: In a large bowl, combine the chopped coriander, gram flour, rice flour, ginger-garlic paste, green chillies, turmeric, red chilli powder, sesame seeds, carom seeds, sugar, lemon juice, and salt. Mix well, adding water gradually, until you get a thick, spoonable batter — thick enough to hold its shape, not runny.

Prepare for steaming: Grease a shallow, heatproof plate or tin (one that fits inside your steamer or a large pot with a steaming rack). Pour the batter in and spread it out evenly, about ¾ inch thick.
Steam: Steam over boiling water for 20–25 minutes, until a knife or toothpick inserted comes out clean. Let it cool completely — this makes slicing much easier.
Slice: Once cooled, cut the steamed slab into small squares or diamonds.

Add tempering (optional): Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a small pan, add mustard seeds, sesame seeds, and curry leaves, and let them sizzle. Pour this over the sliced pieces and toss gently, if you'd like extra flavour before pan-frying.
Pan-fry: Heat the 3 tbsp oil in a wide pan on medium heat. Shallow fry the pieces in batches, turning occasionally, for 4–5 minutes until golden and crisp on all sides.
Serve: Serve warm, with mint chutney or tomato ketchup on the side.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — gram flour, coriander, and spices carry no hidden egg risk. No special sourcing concerns here.
common_mistakes: Not letting the steamed slab cool before slicing causes it to crumble and stick to the knife — patience here really pays off. A batter that's too thin won't set properly during steaming, so keep it thick.
uk_sourcing_notes: Gram flour, rice flour, and carom seeds (ajwain) are all easily found at any Indian grocer or larger supermarket world foods aisle. A steamer basket, idli stand, or even a heatproof plate set on a trivet inside a large lidded pot all work fine for steaming.
storage_notes: The steamed (unfried) slab keeps well refrigerated for 2–3 days — slice and pan-fry fresh batches as needed. Once fried, best eaten the same day, though leftovers can be re-crisped in a dry pan.
kid_friendly_notes: Reduce or omit the green chillies and red chilli powder for a milder version — the sesame and carom seeds still give plenty of flavour without heat.

name: Lemon Rice (Chitranna)
description: Tangy, lightly spiced rice tempered with mustard seeds, peanuts, and curry leaves, finished with fresh lemon juice — a light, quick dish perfect for using up leftover rice.

items.name: rice (raw, uncooked measure — use any regular white rice; cook and cool before using, see method)
red chillies, broken (or 2 green chillies, slit)
lemon juice (about 1 large lemon, adjust to taste)

steps: Cook the rice: If starting with raw rice, cook it as you normally would (boiling or rice cooker) until just done — not mushy, grains should stay separate. Spread it out on a wide plate or tray and let it cool completely, ideally to room temperature. This is essential, as warm rice turns clumpy and mushy when mixed. If using leftover rice, simply fluff it up gently with a fork to separate the grains.
Start the tempering: Heat the oil in a wide pan on medium heat. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter.

Add lentils and spices: Add the urad dal and chana dal, and sauté for about 30 seconds until they turn light golden. Add the cumin seeds, hing, curry leaves, and dried red chillies (or green chillies). Sauté for another 20–30 seconds until fragrant.
Add nuts: Add the peanuts and cashews (if using), and sauté for a minute until lightly golden and toasty.
Add turmeric: Add the turmeric powder and stir for a few seconds — take care not to let it burn.

Combine with rice: Reduce the heat to low. Add the cooled rice and salt to the pan. Using a light hand, gently fold the rice into the tempering (like tossing a salad, not stirring vigorously) until evenly coated and the yellow colour is well distributed.
Finish: Turn off the heat. Add the lemon juice and fresh coriander, and toss gently once more to combine. Taste and adjust salt or lemon juice as needed.
Serve: Serve warm or at room temperature, on its own or with a side of pickle or crisps (papad).

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: This recipe is naturally egg-free — rice, lentils, peanuts, spices, and lemon contain no eggs or hidden egg risk. No special sourcing concerns here.
common_mistakes: Using warm or freshly cooked rice is the most common cause of clumpy, mushy lemon rice — always cool the rice fully (spreading it out on a tray speeds this up) before mixing. Also, add the lemon juice only after the heat is off, as cooking it directly can turn the flavour slightly bitter and dull the tang.
uk_sourcing_notes: Any regular long-grain white rice from a UK supermarket works well; basmati is not traditional here but works fine as a substitute if that's what you have on hand. Urad dal, chana dal, and curry leaves are best sourced from an Indian grocer, though curry leaves can sometimes be found fresh or frozen in larger Tesco/Sainsbury's world foods sections.
storage_notes: This dish is ideal for using up leftover rice and keeps well in the fridge for up to 2 days — great for packed lunches. Serve cold or at room temperature, or reheat gently; avoid over-microwaving as it can dry the rice out.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the dried red or green chillies for a milder version — the lemon and light spices still give plenty of flavour without heat.

name: Malvani Vegetable Curry with Rice Bhakri
description: A spicy, coconut-based curry in the coastal Malvani style, packed with mixed vegetables, served with a hand-patted rice flour flatbread.

items.name: –3 tbsp Malvani masala (shop-bought paste or powder)
grated fresh coconut (or desiccated coconut, soaked in 4 tbsp warm water)
Water, as needed to thin the gravy
rice flour, plus extra for dusting

steps: Temper: Heat the oil in a pan on medium heat. Add mustard seeds and curry leaves, letting them sizzle.
Cook onion: Add the onion and cook until golden, about 4–5 minutes.
Add aromatics: Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add masala: Add the Malvani masala and turmeric, stirring constantly for 1–2 minutes (add a splash of water if it starts to catch on the pan).
Add tomatoes: Add the tomatoes and cook until soft and the oil separates, about 5–6 minutes.
Add coconut: Stir in the coconut (and its soaking water, if using desiccated) and cook for 2–3 minutes.

Finish: Adjust consistency with a splash more water if needed, and stir in the fresh coriander.
9. Bind the dough: Place the rice flour and salt in a bowl. Gradually add hot water, mixing with a spoon first, then knead once cool enough to handle into a smooth, soft dough.
10. Divide: Divide into 6–8 balls.

11. Pat out: Pat each ball by hand on a damp cloth or lightly greased plastic sheet into a round disc about ¼ inch thick — rice flour dough is fragile and doesn't roll well with a pin, so patting by hand is traditional.

12. Cook: Carefully transfer to a hot, dry tawa. Cook on medium heat, flipping once the underside sets, then cook both sides, pressing gently with a cloth, until light golden spots appear and it's cooked through, about 2–3 minutes per side.

storage_notes: The curry keeps 2 days refrigerated and improves in flavour overnight. Bhakri is best fresh — it hardens once cooled and doesn't store well.
kid_friendly_notes: Malvani masala is quite pungent and spicy — reduce the quantity significantly for children, or stir in a little extra coconut to mellow the heat.

name: Masala Avocado Toast
description: A quick fusion breakfast — creamy mashed avocado spiked with Indian spices and tempered with a mustard-cumin tadka, piled onto crisp toasted bread.

items.name: –10 curry leaves (optional, but adds authentic flavour)
tomato, finely chopped (deseeded if you prefer less liquid)
of bread of your choice (sourdough or granary work well)
A few thin slices of red onion or radish, for garnish (optional)
A light sprinkle of chilli flakes or extra chaat masala, for garnish (optional)

steps: Make the tempering: Heat the oil or ghee in a small pan on medium heat. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add cumin seeds, hing, curry leaves, and green chilli. Sauté for about 30 seconds until fragrant, then turn off the heat and let it cool slightly.
Mash the avocado: Halve and deseed the avocados, scoop the flesh into a bowl, and mash roughly with a fork — keep it a little chunky rather than completely smooth.
Combine: Add the tomato, red onion, chaat masala, red chilli powder, roasted cumin powder, lemon juice, and salt to the mashed avocado. Mix gently to combine.
Add the tempering: Pour the cooled tempering (oil and all) over the avocado mixture and fold it through. Stir in the fresh coriander.
Toast the bread: Toast the bread slices until golden and crisp, either in a toaster or on a hot griddle with a very light brushing of oil or ghee for extra flavour.
Assemble: Generously spread or pile the masala avocado mash onto each slice of toast. Garnish with thin onion or radish slices and a sprinkle of chilli flakes or chaat masala, if using.
Serve immediately while the toast is still crisp.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 2 slices of toast with topping.

kid_friendly_notes: Omit the green chilli and reduce the red chilli powder for a milder, kid-friendly version — the cumin and garam masala still give plenty of flavour without reheating it

name: Masala Beans on Toast Sandwich
description: A spiced Indian twist on classic beans on toast, turned into a hearty grilled sandwich with tangy, gently spiced baked beans.

items.name: Salt, to taste (go easy, as baked beans are often already salted)
of bread of your choice (check label — see egg-check note)

steps: Make the masala: Heat the oil in a pan on medium heat. Add cumin seeds and let them sizzle. Add the onion and cook for 3–4 minutes until softened.
Add aromatics: Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for 30 seconds.
Add tomato and spices: Add the tomato, turmeric, and chilli powder. Cook for 3–4 minutes until the tomato softens.

Add beans: Stir in the baked beans and garam masala. Simmer for 4–5 minutes, mashing lightly with the back of a spoon to slightly thicken the mixture. Season with salt if needed and stir in coriander.
Assemble: Spread the masala beans generously over 4 slices of bread. Sprinkle with grated cheese, if using, and top with the remaining slices.
Grill: Butter the outside of each sandwich lightly, then toast in a pan or sandwich press on medium heat for 2–3 minutes per side, until golden and crisp, and the cheese has melted.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 1 full sandwich per serving.

storage_notes: The masala beans mixture keeps 2 days refrigerated and reheats well — great for making ahead and assembling fresh sandwiches as needed. Assembled sandwiches are best grilled fresh, not stored.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the chilli powder and use a milder garam masala quantity — kids often enjoy this as a comforting, only lightly spiced version of a familiar favourite.

name: Masala Cheese & Sweetcorn Sandwich
description: A creamy, lightly spiced cheese and sweetcorn filling grilled between crisp bread — a popular Indian café-style toastie with a comforting, mild kick.

items.name: grated cheese (cheddar or a mild melting cheese)
mayonnaise-style eggless dressing or thick yoghurt (see egg-check note)
of bread of your choice (check label — see egg-check note)

steps: Make the filling: In a bowl, combine the sweetcorn, grated cheese, mayonnaise or yoghurt, red onion, coriander, green chilli (if using), chaat masala, red chilli powder, black pepper, and salt. Mix well until evenly combined.
Assemble: Spread the filling generously over 4 slices of bread, and top with the remaining slices.
Grill: Butter the outside of each sandwich lightly, then toast in a pan or sandwich press on medium heat for 2–3 minutes per side, until golden and crisp, and the cheese has melted through.
Serve: Slice in half and serve hot.

name: Masala Dosa (South Indian)
description: A crisp, golden fermented rice-and-lentil crepe wrapped around a lightly spiced potato filling — a South Indian classic, best enjoyed with coconut chutney and sambar.

items.name: rice (idli rice or regular white rice)
Water, as needed for soaking, grinding, and thinning (see method)
Oil or ghee, for cooking the dosas (roughly ½ tsp per dosa)

steps: Making the batter (start a day ahead)

Soak: In one bowl, combine the rice, chana dal, and poha; in another, combine the urad dal and fenugreek seeds. Rinse each 2–3 times, then cover with water (enough to fully submerge, roughly a couple of inches above the grains) and soak separately for 4–6 hours.

Grind: Drain both. Grind the urad dal–fenugreek mixture first, adding water a little at a time (roughly 2 tbsp at a time) until you get a smooth, thick, fluffy batter. Transfer to a large bowl. Grind the rice mixture similarly until mostly smooth with a slight grain, adding water gradually as needed. Combine both batters in the large bowl and mix well with your hand (this helps fermentation) for a minute or two.

Ferment: Cover the bowl loosely and leave in a warm place for 8–14 hours (or overnight), until the batter has risen and looks bubbly and airy. In a cold UK kitchen, this can take longer — an oven with just the light on, or near a radiator, helps.
Finish the batter: Once fermented, stir in salt to taste. The batter should be of a pourable, thick-cream consistency — thin with a splash of water (a tbsp at a time) if it's too thick.
Making the potato masala filling

Temper the spices: Heat the oil in a pan on medium heat. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add cumin seeds, urad dal, and chana dal, and sauté for about 30 seconds until the dals turn light golden.
Add aromatics: Add hing, curry leaves, and green chillies. Sauté for 20–30 seconds.
Cook the onion: Add the sliced onion and cook for 4–5 minutes until soft and translucent.

Add potatoes: Roughly mash the boiled potatoes by hand (keep some texture, not smooth) and add to the pan along with turmeric and salt. Mix well, mashing further into the spices, and cook for 3–4 minutes until everything is well combined and heated through. Add a splash of water (2–3 tbsp) if it looks too dry.
Finish: Turn off the heat, stir in lemon juice and coriander leaves. Set aside, keeping warm.
Making the dosas
Heat the pan: Heat a flat non-stick or cast-iron griddle (tawa) on medium-high heat. Test readiness by sprinkling a few drops of water — they should sizzle and evaporate quickly.

Pour and spread: Pour a ladleful (roughly 4 tbsp) of batter in the centre. Using the back of the ladle, spread it outward in a circular motion from the centre, working quickly to form a thin, even circle.
Cook: Drizzle ½ tsp of oil or ghee around the edges. Cook for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp, and the edges start lifting.

Fill and fold: Place about 2–3 tbsp of the potato filling along the centre of the dosa. Fold both sides over the filling (or roll it up) and slide onto a plate. Repeat with the remaining batter and filling.
Serve: Serve immediately while crisp, ideally with coconut chutney and sambar on the side.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 2 dosas with filling per serving.
egg_check_notes: Every component here — rice, lentils, potatoes, spices, oil — is naturally egg-free. No hidden-egg risk in this recipe as long as you're making the batter from scratch. (If ever buying ready-made dosa batter from a UK Indian grocer, it's almost always egg-free by tradition, but check the label if it's a newer or unfamiliar brand.)
common_mistakes: Skipping the fenugreek seeds — they help fermentation and give the batter its slightly tangy flavour. Not spreading the dosa fast enough — the batter starts cooking the moment it hits the pan, so work quickly and confidently in one continuous spiral. Flipping too early — let the base fully crisp and lift naturally at the edges before folding. UK adaptation: Idli rice can be hard to find outside Indian grocers — parboiled/"easy cook" rice from a supermarket is a reasonable substitute, though texture will be slightly less airy. A blender or food processor works fine instead of a traditional wet grinder, just grind in batches so the motor doesn't strain. Fermentation in UK weather: Cold homes (especially in winter) slow fermentation significantly. If your batter hasn't risen after 14 hours, leave it longer — it can take up to 24 hours in a cold kitchen. Don't discard it; South Indian batters are forgiving.
storage_notes: The batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days (it gets tangier with time, which some prefer). The potato filling keeps for 2 days refrigerated — reheat gently before using. Dosas themselves are best made fresh and don't reheat well.
kid_friendly_notes: Reduce or omit green chillies in the potato filling for a milder version; you can also serve plain dosa (no filling) with a mild chutney for younger children

name: Masala Hash Browns
description: Crispy, golden potato hash browns given an Indian twist with warming spices, green chilli, and coriander — a fun fusion breakfast side.

items.name: potatoes (starchy, like Maris Piper), peeled and coarsely grated
ajwain (carom seeds, optional — helps digestion and adds flavour)
gram flour (besan) or cornflour, as a binder

steps: Grate and drain: Coarsely grate the potatoes into a large bowl of cold water (this prevents browning and rinses off excess surface starch). Swish briefly, then drain thoroughly.

Remove moisture: Transfer the grated potato to a clean kitchen towel or muslin cloth and squeeze out as much water as possible — this step is essential for crispy hash browns rather than soggy ones. Let it sit for 10 minutes, then squeeze again.

Season the mixture: In a large bowl, combine the drained potato with the onion, green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds, turmeric, red chilli powder, garam masala, ajwain (if using), and coriander leaves. Mix well.

Bind: Sprinkle over the gram flour or cornflour and salt, then mix thoroughly until the mixture holds together when pressed — it shouldn't be wet or loose. If it still feels too wet, add another ½ tbsp of gram flour.

Shape: Divide the mixture into 8 portions. Take each portion in your palms and press firmly into a flat, compact patty about the size of your palm — the tighter you pack it, the better it holds together while frying.
Heat the oil: Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a wide, flat pan or griddle on medium heat.

Fry the hash browns: Place 3–4 patties in the pan at a time, without overcrowding. Cook for 4–5 minutes per side, pressing down gently once with a spatula, until deep golden brown and crisp on both sides. Add the remaining oil as needed for the second batch.
Drain and serve: Transfer to a plate lined with kitchen paper to remove excess oil. Serve hot, as is or with ketchup, mint chutney, or a dollop of yoghurt.

uk_sourcing_notes: Maris Piper or King Edward potatoes (widely available at any UK supermarket) work best due to their higher starch content, which helps crispiness. Ajwain is available at Indian grocers; if you don't have it, it can simply be left out without much impact on the dish.
storage_notes: The shaped (uncooked) patties can be covered and refrigerated for a few hours before frying. Cooked hash browns are best eaten fresh and crisp, but leftovers can be reheated in a dry pan or air fryer to re-crisp — avoid the microwave, which makes them soggy.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the green chilli and reduce the red chilli powder for a milder, kid-friendly version — the cumin and garam masala still give plenty of flavour without heat.

name: Methi Thepla Roll with Pickle
description: Soft, spiced fenugreek-leaf flatbreads rolled up with a smear of pickle — a simple, portable Gujarati favourite, popular for travel and lunchboxes.

items.name: fresh fenugreek (methi) leaves, finely chopped (or 2 tbsp dried fenugreek/kasoori methi, soaked briefly in water)
mixed pickle (achaar) of choice, e.g. mango or mixed vegetable

Mix well, then gradually add water and knead into a smooth, slightly firm dough (firmer than roti dough, as thepla should be sturdy enough to roll and travel well).
Divide: Divide the dough into 8 balls.
Roll: Roll each ball out into a thin, even round on a lightly floured surface.

Cook: Heat a tawa on medium heat. Cook each thepla for about a minute, until small bubbles appear, then flip. Brush lightly with oil on both sides and cook, pressing gently, until golden-brown spots form on both sides, about 2–3 minutes total.

Roll and serve: Roll up tightly and serve warm, or pack for travel/lunch once cooled.

uk_sourcing_notes: Fresh methi (fenugreek leaves) is available at Indian grocers, sometimes fresh, sometimes frozen — dried kasoori methi is a reliable pantry substitute and widely available. Ajwain and sesame seeds are also at any Indian grocer.
storage_notes: Thepla is famous for travelling well — it keeps for 2–3 days at room temperature (wrapped in a cloth or foil) and up to a week refrigerated, making it ideal for long journeys or packed lunches.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the green chilli and reduce red chilli powder for a milder version — pair with a milder, sweeter pickle (like mango) for kids who prefer less heat.

name: Modak
description: Soft, delicate rice flour dumplings steamed and filled with a sweet coconut-jaggery filling — the beloved festive sweet made especially for Ganesh Chaturthi.

items.name: fresh grated coconut (or desiccated coconut, soaked in 4 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes)

steps: Make the filling: Heat 1 tsp ghee in a pan on medium heat. Add the grated coconut and jaggery, and cook, stirring continuously, for 6–8 minutes until the mixture thickens and the jaggery is fully melted and combined — it should hold together when pressed but not be wet.
Finish the filling: Stir in the cardamom powder, nutmeg (if using), and poppy seeds. Let it cool completely before shaping.

Make the dough: In a pan, bring the water to a boil with the ghee and salt. Once boiling, reduce heat to low and add the rice flour all at once, stirring quickly and continuously to avoid lumps. Cover and let it steam-cook on the lowest heat for 2 minutes.

Knead: Turn the dough out onto a plate. Once cool enough to handle (but still warm), knead it with lightly greased hands until smooth and pliable, adding a few drops of water if it feels dry or cracks.

Shape: Divide the dough into 12 portions and keep covered with a damp cloth to prevent drying. Take one portion, grease your palms lightly, and flatten it into a small disc, either in your palm or using a modak mould.

Fill: Place a spoonful of the coconut-jaggery filling in the centre. Gently bring the edges up and pleat them together at the top, pinching to seal into the traditional pointed modak shape (or simply press together neatly if pleating feels tricky — taste matters more than shape).
Steam: Arrange the shaped modaks on a greased steamer plate or idli stand, ensuring they don't touch. Steam over boiling water for 10–12 minutes until they look glossy and slightly translucent.
Serve: Let cool slightly before serving, traditionally with a drizzle of ghee on top.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 3 modaks per serving.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — rice flour, coconut, and jaggery carry no hidden egg risk.
common_mistakes: Overcooking the dough or letting it cool too much before shaping makes it crack and hard to pleat — work with it while still warm. A filling that's too wet makes the modak soggy — cook it until it properly holds together.
uk_sourcing_notes: Rice flour is at any Indian grocer or supermarket baking aisle. Fresh coconut can be found at larger supermarkets or Indian/Caribbean grocers; desiccated coconut (soaked before use) is a reliable substitute and widely available everywhere.

kid_friendly_notes: No heat in this dish at all — naturally kid-friendly as is. Poppy seeds can be omitted if unavailable or not preferred.

name: Paneer Tikka Wrap
description: Smoky, spice-marinated grilled paneer and peppers rolled up in a soft tortilla with crunchy salad and a cooling mint-yoghurt sauce — a handy fusion take on paneer tikka, perfect for lunch on the go.

items.name: (about 300g block, cut into cubes) paneer — see note on spoon-measuring below
ginger-garlic paste (or ½ tsp each grated ginger and garlic)
Kashmiri red chilli powder (for colour and mild heat)
red or green pepper, cut into chunky squares
fresh mint leaves, finely chopped (or 1 tbsp mint sauce as a substitute)
tortillas or wraps (check label — see egg-check note)
oil, for cooking the paneer and veg
onion, thinly sliced (for filling, separate from grilling onion)
tomato, thinly sliced or deseeded and chopped
