steps: Marinating

Make the marinade: In a large bowl, whisk together the yoghurt, gram flour, oil, ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri chilli powder, turmeric, garam masala, roasted cumin powder, lemon juice, and salt until smooth.

Coat: Add the paneer cubes, onion petals, and pepper squares to the marinade. Toss gently to coat everything evenly, being careful not to break the paneer. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes (longer, up to a few hours, deepens the flavour).
Making the mint-yoghurt sauce
Combine: In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt, mint, coriander, roasted cumin powder, chaat masala, lemon juice, and salt. Stir well and refrigerate until ready to serve.
Cooking the paneer tikka
Heat the pan: Heat the oil in a wide pan or griddle on medium-high heat.

Cook: Add the marinated paneer, onion, and pepper pieces in a single layer (cook in batches if needed to avoid overcrowding). Cook for 6–8 minutes, turning occasionally, until the paneer is lightly charred at the edges and the vegetables are just softened with a bit of bite left.
Assembling the wraps
Warm the tortillas: Heat each tortilla briefly in a dry pan or directly over a low flame for a few seconds on each side, until soft and pliable with a few light char spots.
Layer: Spread a spoonful of the mint-yoghurt sauce down the centre of each tortilla. Top with a portion of the shredded cabbage, sliced onion, and tomato.
Add the tikka: Spoon over the grilled paneer, onion, and pepper mixture.
Finish and roll: Add a final squeeze of lemon juice, then fold in the sides of the tortilla and roll it up tightly, like a burrito. Slice in half if desired.
Serve immediately, with any extra mint-yoghurt sauce on the side for dipping.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 1 wrap per serving.
common_mistakes: Overcooking the paneer makes it rubbery — cook just until lightly charred, as it firms up further off the heat. Also, don't skip patting the paneer dry-ish after marinating if it looks very wet, as excess moisture can make it steam rather than char in the pan.
uk_sourcing_notes: Paneer is available fresh or frozen at any Indian grocer, and pre-packed at most large Tesco/Sainsbury's/Asda stores in the world foods or chilled section. Kashmiri chilli powder gives the classic red colour without too much heat — regular chilli powder works but use slightly less and expect a browner colour.
storage_notes: The paneer can marinate up to 24 hours ahead, covered in the fridge — flavour improves the longer it sits. The mint-yoghurt sauce keeps for 2 days refrigerated. Assembled wraps are best eaten fresh; if packing for lunch, keep the sauce separate and add just before eating to avoid a soggy wrap.
kid_friendly_notes: Use plain chilli powder in a smaller quantity, or omit entirely, for a milder version — the yoghurt marinade keeps the paneer flavourful even without heat.

name: Paneer Tikka Paratha Roll
description: Spiced grilled paneer and peppers rolled up inside a flaky whole wheat paratha with crunchy salad and mint-yoghurt sauce — a handheld, portable twist on paneer tikka.

items.name: whole wheat flour (atta), plus extra for dusting
ghee or oil, for cooking (roughly 1 tbsp per paratha)

steps: Marinate: Whisk together the yoghurt, gram flour, oil, ginger-garlic paste, chilli powder, turmeric, garam masala, cumin powder, lemon juice, and salt. Add the paneer, onion, and pepper, tossing gently to coat. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.
Make the mint sauce: Mix yoghurt, mint, coriander, cumin powder, chaat masala, lemon juice, and salt. Refrigerate until needed.
Knead the paratha dough: Combine flour, salt, and oil, then gradually add water and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

Cook the paneer: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan on medium-high heat. Add the marinated paneer, onion, and pepper, cooking for 6–8 minutes, turning occasionally, until lightly charred and just cooked through.
Roll the parathas: Divide the dough into 4 balls. Roll each out into a large, thin round.
Cook the parathas: Cook each on a hot tawa for about a minute per side, brushing with ghee or oil on both sides, until golden with light brown spots.
Assemble: Lay a warm paratha flat. Spread a spoonful of mint-yoghurt sauce down the centre, then layer with shredded cabbage, sliced onion, and the paneer tikka mixture.
Roll and serve: Add a squeeze of lemon juice, then roll up tightly. Slice in half and serve immediately, with extra mint sauce on the side.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — paneer, atta, yoghurt, and spices carry no hidden egg risk, and unlike a tortilla-based wrap, homemade paratha removes the need to check a shop-bought wrap label entirely.
common_mistakes: Overcooking the paneer makes it rubbery — cook just until lightly charred. Rolling the paratha too thick makes it difficult to fold around the filling neatly.
uk_sourcing_notes: Paneer and atta are both at any Indian grocer or larger Tesco/Sainsbury's world foods aisle.
storage_notes: Paneer can marinate up to 24 hours ahead. Parathas can be made ahead and reheated on a dry tawa. Assemble fresh for best texture, or pack the roll wrapped in foil for lunch.
kid_friendly_notes: Use a smaller quantity of chilli powder for a milder version — the yoghurt marinade keeps it flavourful regardless.

name: Puran Poli (Sweet, Dessert-Style)
description: A soft, flaky flatbread stuffed with a sweet spiced lentil filling and cooked with ghee — a festive Maharashtrian classic, best enjoyed warm with a drizzle of ghee or a side of milk.

items.name: Water, as needed for boiling (enough to cover dal by about 2 inches)
plain flour or a mix of plain flour and whole wheat flour
oil, plus more for resting the dough
ghee (roughly ½ tbsp per puran poli)

steps: Making the puran (filling)

Boil the dal: In a pot, combine the chana dal with enough water to cover by about 2 inches. Boil until very soft and mushy, about 25–30 minutes (or 3–4 whistles in a pressure cooker). Drain any excess water thoroughly (reserve it — it makes a lovely base for a simple dal soup another day, but isn't used in this recipe).

Cook with jaggery: Return the drained dal to the pan with the ghee and jaggery. Cook on low-medium heat, mashing and stirring continuously, for 8–10 minutes until the mixture thickens into a dry, mouldable paste that holds its shape — this takes patience, as the jaggery releases moisture initially.
Flavour: Stir in the cardamom and nutmeg (if using). Let the puran cool completely, then divide into 8 portions and roll into smooth balls.
Making the dough
Knead: Combine the flour, turmeric, oil, and salt. Gradually add water, kneading into a very soft, slightly sticky dough — softer than regular roti dough.
Rest: Cover with a little oil brushed on top and let it rest for at least 30 minutes.
Assembling and cooking
Divide: Divide the dough into 8 portions, slightly smaller than the puran balls, and roll into smooth balls.
Stuff: Flatten a dough ball into a small disc, place a puran ball in the centre, and bring the edges up and over to seal completely, pinching at the top. Flatten gently into a ball again.
Roll out: Dust lightly with flour and gently roll the stuffed ball into a thin, even round, about the size of a small side plate — go slowly and evenly to avoid the filling breaking through.
Cook: Heat a tawa on medium heat. Place the rolled puran poli on it and cook for about a minute until small bubbles appear.

Flip and add ghee: Flip, spread ½ tsp ghee over the top, and cook for another minute. Flip again, add ghee to the other side, and cook, pressing gently, until both sides have light golden-brown spots, 3–4 minutes total.
Repeat: Keep cooked puran poli warm, wrapped in a cloth. Repeat with the remaining portions.
Serve: Serve warm, with an extra drizzle of ghee or a glass of warm milk on the side.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 2 puran poli per serving.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — chana dal, jaggery, flour, and ghee carry no hidden egg risk.
common_mistakes: Not cooking the puran filling dry enough is the most common cause of it bursting through the dough while rolling — it should hold together firmly, not be soft or wet. Rolling too aggressively or too thin also risks tearing.
uk_sourcing_notes: Chana dal and jaggery are both at any Indian grocer. Jaggery is sometimes labelled "gur" — either block or granulated forms work fine here.
storage_notes: The puran filling can be made 1–2 days ahead and refrigerated. Cooked puran poli keep for 2 days refrigerated; reheat gently on a dry tawa with a touch of ghee, not the microwave, to preserve texture.
kid_friendly_notes: No heat in this dish — naturally kid-friendly. Cardamom can be reduced slightly if a milder flavour is preferred for younger children.

name: Schezwan Noodles
description: Fiery, garlicky stir-fried noodles tossed in a spicy Schezwan sauce with crunchy vegetables — a fast, punchy Indo-Chinese street-food favourite.

items.name: dried noodles, uncooked measure (plain wheat "hakka" noodles or rice noodles — check label, see egg-check note)
oil (for tossing cooked noodles, to prevent sticking)

ingredients.group: For the Schezwan sauce (can be made ahead)

items.name: –12 dried red chillies, soaked in hot water for 20 minutes
–3 tbsp water, as needed to blend
spring onion, sliced (white and green parts separated)
Salt, to taste (go easy, as soy sauce is salty)

steps: Making the Schezwan sauce
Blend the chillies: Drain the soaked dried red chillies and blend them with 2–3 tbsp water into a smooth, thick paste.
Cook the paste: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a small pan on medium heat. Add the chopped garlic and ginger, and sauté for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chilli paste: Add the blended red chilli paste and cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring often, until the raw smell disappears and the oil starts to separate slightly at the edges.

Season: Stir in the ketchup, soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, and salt. Cook for another 1–2 minutes until well combined and glossy. Set aside (this makes a slightly larger batch than needed — extra keeps well, see storage note).
Cooking the noodles

Boil: Cook the noodles in a large pot of salted boiling water according to the packet instructions, until just tender but still with a slight bite (al dente). Drain and rinse briefly under cold water to stop the cooking and remove excess starch.
Toss with oil: Toss the drained noodles with 1 tsp oil to prevent them from sticking together while you prepare the stir-fry.
Stir-frying
Heat the wok: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large pan or wok on high heat until just starting to shimmer.
Add aromatics: Add the chopped garlic, ginger, and the white parts of the spring onion. Stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add vegetables: Add the onion, pepper, carrot, and cabbage. Stir-fry on high heat for 2–3 minutes, keeping the vegetables crunchy rather than soft.
Add sauce: Add 3–4 tbsp of the prepared Schezwan sauce (adjust to your spice preference — add more for extra heat) along with the soy sauce and vinegar. Toss to coat the vegetables evenly.
Add noodles: Add the boiled noodles to the pan. Using tongs or two spatulas, toss everything together on high heat for 2–3 minutes until the noodles are evenly coated in the sauce and heated through.
Finish: Taste and adjust salt or add a touch more Schezwan sauce if you'd like it spicier. Garnish with the green parts of the spring onion.
Serve immediately, while hot.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
common_mistakes: Overcooking the noodles before stir-frying makes them mushy and prone to breaking apart in the wok — slightly undercook them at the boiling stage since they'll cook a little further during stir-frying. Also, letting the vegetables overcook loses the signature crunch that makes this dish satisfying.
uk_sourcing_notes: Dried red chillies, soy sauce, and vinegar are all easily found in the world foods aisle of any UK supermarket. Egg-free hakka or rice noodles are reliably found at Indian or Chinese grocers — if using a supermarket "straight-to-wok" noodle pack, double check the label as some brands do include egg.
storage_notes: The Schezwan sauce keeps well refrigerated in an airtight container for up to a week, and makes a versatile base for other Indo-Chinese dishes too. The noodles themselves are best eaten fresh, though leftovers can be reheated in a hot pan with a splash of water to loosen them — avoid the microwave, which can make them clump.
kid_friendly_notes: Reduce the number of dried red chillies in the sauce (or reduce the quantity of sauce used in the stir-fry) for a much milder version — a little extra ketchup helps balance the flavour without the heat.

name: Sev Puri
description: Crisp flat puris topped with spiced potato, onion, chutneys, and a generous shower of crunchy sev — a beloved bite-sized Mumbai chaat.

steps: Make the tamarind chutney: Simmer the tamarind pulp, jaggery, chilli powder, cumin powder, salt, and water in a small pan for 5–6 minutes until slightly thickened. Cool before using.
Make the mint chutney: Blend the mint, coriander, green chilli, lemon juice, salt, and water into a smooth paste.
Arrange the puris: Lay the flat puris out on a large serving plate or tray, indent-side up.
Top with potato and onion: Place a small spoonful of diced potato on each puri, followed by a little chopped onion and tomato.
Add chutneys: Drizzle each puri with a little tamarind chutney and mint chutney.
Finish: Sprinkle chaat masala and a light dusting of red chilli powder over the top, then generously scatter sev and coriander leaves over everything.
Serve immediately: Sev puri must be eaten right away, before the puris soften.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 6 puris per serving.
common_mistakes: Assembling too far in advance is the main pitfall — the puris turn soft and lose their signature crunch within minutes of adding chutney. Prep everything else ahead, assemble last.
uk_sourcing_notes: Papdi and sev are both sold at any Indian grocer in the snacks aisle. Tamarind pulp is also there or in larger supermarket world foods sections.
storage_notes: Both chutneys and the boiled potato keep well refrigerated for a few days. Only assemble the puris just before serving.
kid_friendly_notes: Skip the green chilli in the mint chutney and the red chilli powder garnish for a milder version.

name: Shrikhand
description: A rich, sweetened, and lightly spiced strained yoghurt dessert, flavoured with saffron and cardamom — a Maharashtrian festive classic, best served chilled.

steps: Strain the yoghurt: Line a sieve with a muslin cloth or clean thin tea towel and set it over a bowl. Pour in the yoghurt, gather the edges of the cloth, and tie loosely. Refrigerate and let it strain for 6–8 hours or overnight, until thick and most of the whey has drained off — you should be left with a firm, creamy hung curd (chakka).
Sweeten: Transfer the strained yoghurt to a bowl. Add the sugar and whisk well until smooth and the sugar has fully dissolved — this can take a few minutes of steady whisking.
Flavour: Stir in the saffron-soaked milk and cardamom powder, mixing until evenly combined and the shrikhand turns a pale golden colour.
Chill: Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour before serving, to let the flavours settle.
Serve: Spoon into small bowls and garnish with chopped pistachios, almonds, and a few extra saffron strands.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free — yoghurt, sugar, and nuts carry no hidden egg risk.
common_mistakes: Not straining the yoghurt long enough leaves the shrikhand runny rather than thick and spoonable — don't rush this step. Using low-fat yoghurt gives a much less rich, less traditional result.
uk_sourcing_notes: Use a good full-fat plain yoghurt or Greek yoghurt from any UK supermarket — Greek yoghurt is already quite thick and can shorten straining time slightly. Saffron and pistachios are at any Indian grocer or larger supermarket.
storage_notes: Shrikhand keeps well refrigerated for 3–4 days in an airtight container, and the flavour deepens over the first day. Freezing isn't recommended, as it affects the texture.
kid_friendly_notes: No heat in this dish — naturally kid-friendly. Some families add a little mango pulp to make "aamrakhand," a popular seasonal variation, if you'd like to try a variant.

name: Vada Pav
description: A spiced potato fritter (batata vada) sandwiched in a soft bread roll with chutneys — Mumbai's iconic street food burger.

items.name: A pinch of baking soda (optional, for extra crispness)
Water, as needed to make a smooth, thick coating batter
Oil, for deep or shallow frying
bread rolls or pav (check label, see egg-check note)
mint-coriander chutney (blend mint, coriander, green chilli, lemon juice, salt, water)
dry garlic chutney (garlic, dried red chilli powder, roasted peanuts or desiccated coconut, ground together with salt)

steps: Make the potato filling: Heat the oil in a pan on medium heat. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add cumin seeds, hing, and curry leaves.
Add aromatics: Add the ginger-garlic paste and green chillies, sauté for 30 seconds.

Combine with potato: Add the mashed potato, turmeric, and salt. Mix well, mashing further into the spices, and cook for 2–3 minutes until well combined. Turn off heat, stir in lemon juice and coriander.
Shape: Once cool enough to handle, divide the mixture into 8 portions and roll into balls, then flatten slightly.
Make the batter: Whisk the gram flour, turmeric, hing, baking soda (if using), and salt with water until you get a smooth, thick, coating batter — similar to pancake batter consistency.

Fry: Heat oil for deep frying in a pan. Dip each potato ball into the batter, coating fully, and carefully lower into the hot oil. Fry in batches for 4–5 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper.
Make the garlic chutney: Blend the garlic, dried red chilli powder, roasted peanuts (or coconut), and salt into a coarse, dry mixture.
Assemble: Slice each bread roll almost in half (not all the way through). Spread mint chutney on one side and a little dry garlic chutney on the other.
Fill: Place one vada inside each roll, pressing down gently to close.
Serve immediately, with fried green chillies on the side if desired.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 1 vada pav per serving.
common_mistakes: Batter that's too thin won't coat the vada properly and can make it greasy — it should be thick enough to cling. Overcrowding the frying oil drops the temperature and results in soggy, oily vada rather than crisp ones.
uk_sourcing_notes: Look for "pav" specifically at Indian grocers for the most authentic result and lowest egg risk. Gram flour (besan) is at any Indian grocer or larger supermarket world foods aisle.
storage_notes: The potato filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated. Fried vada are best eaten fresh, but can be re-crisped in an air fryer or hot oven if needed. The dry garlic chutney keeps well in an airtight container for weeks.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the green chillies from the filling and use less garlic chutney (which can be quite fiery) for a milder version.

name: Veg Fried Rice with Manchurian Gravy
description: Soft vegetable-studded fried rice served with deep-fried vegetable balls smothered in a glossy, tangy-spicy Manchurian gravy — a hearty Indo-Chinese restaurant favourite, fully vegetarian and egg-free.

items.name: Salt and black pepper, to taste
–3 tbsp water, only if needed to bind (add gradually — the vegetables usually release enough moisture)
Oil, for deep or shallow frying
soy sauce (check label — see egg-check note)
cornflour, mixed with 2 tbsp water (for thickening)
rice (raw, uncooked measure — long-grain or basmati; cook and cool before using)
finely chopped mixed vegetables (carrot, French beans, sweetcorn — diced small)
onions, sliced (white and green parts separated)
Salt, to taste (go easy, as soy sauce is already salty)

steps: Vegetable Manchurian Balls
Mix the vegetables: In a large bowl, combine the cabbage, carrot, French beans, spring onion, ginger, garlic, and green chilli.

Bind: Add the cornflour, plain flour, salt, and black pepper. Mix and press the mixture together with your hands — the vegetables should release enough moisture to bind on their own. Only add water a little at a time if the mixture feels too dry to hold together.
Shape: Take small portions of the mixture and roll firmly between your palms into balls about the size of a walnut. You should get around 16 balls.

Fry: Heat oil in a pan (enough for shallow or deep frying). Fry the balls in batches on medium heat for 4–5 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden brown and crisp all over. Drain on kitchen paper.
Manchurian Gravy
Prepare the sauce mix: In a small bowl, combine the soy sauce, ketchup, red chilli sauce, vinegar, and sugar with the 12 tbsp water. Set aside.
Start the stir-fry: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large pan or wok on high heat. Add the chopped garlic, ginger, and green chillies, and stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add vegetables: Add the onion petals and pepper squares. Stir-fry for 2 minutes, keeping them crunchy rather than soft.

Add sauce base: Pour in the prepared sauce mixture and bring to a gentle boil. Add the cornflour-water mixture in a thin stream, stirring continuously, and simmer for 2–3 minutes until the gravy thickens to a glossy, slightly clingy consistency. Adjust salt to taste.

Add the balls: Just before serving, add the fried Manchurian balls to the gravy and toss gently to coat — do this right before serving so the balls stay crisp rather than turning soggy from sitting in the sauce. Garnish with sliced spring onion greens.
Vegetable Fried Rice
Cook the rice: If starting with raw rice, cook until just done, with grains separate. Spread on a tray and cool completely — ideally done well ahead, as warm rice turns mushy when stir-fried.

Stir-fry the vegetables: Heat the oil in a large pan or wok on high heat. Add the garlic and stir-fry for 20–30 seconds. Add the mixed diced vegetables and white parts of the spring onion, and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until just tender with a slight bite.
Add cabbage: Add the shredded cabbage and stir-fry for another minute.
Add rice: Add the cooled rice and, using a folding motion, toss it through the vegetables so the grains stay separate.
Season: Add the soy sauce, vinegar, black pepper, and salt (if needed). Toss on high heat for 2–3 minutes until evenly combined. Garnish with the spring onion greens.
Serving
Serve: Plate the fried rice with the Manchurian balls and gravy spooned generously over or alongside. Serve immediately while both are hot.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
common_mistakes: Adding the Manchurian balls to the gravy too early (or letting them sit in it for too long before serving) makes them go soft and soggy — combine just before serving. Overworking or adding too much water to the ball mixture makes them fall apart while frying — the vegetables' natural moisture is usually enough to bind them. Using warm rice for the fried rice leads to a mushy, clumped texture — always cool it fully first.
uk_sourcing_notes: All vegetables, soy sauce, ketchup, and chilli sauce are easily found at any UK supermarket. Cornflour is a standard baking-aisle staple.
storage_notes: The Manchurian balls can be fried ahead and refrigerated for a day, then re-crisped in a hot pan or air fryer before tossing in fresh gravy. The gravy base (without the balls) keeps for 2 days refrigerated. Cooked, cooled rice also keeps well for a day. Assemble everything fresh just before serving for the best texture.
kid_friendly_notes: Reduce or omit the green chillies and red chilli sauce in the gravy for a much milder version — a little extra ketchup helps keep the flavour balanced without the heat.

name: Veg Kolhapuri
description: A fiery, deeply spiced vegetable curry made with a roasted dried red chilli and coconut-based Kolhapuri masala — a popular vegetarian take on Kolhapur's famously bold cuisine.

items.name: –8 dried Kashmiri red chillies (for colour), soaked in hot water for 15 minutes
–3 regular dried red chillies (for heat), soaked alongside
grated fresh coconut (or desiccated coconut, soaked)

steps: Roast the whole spices: Dry roast the coriander seeds, cumin seeds, peppercorns, cloves, and cinnamon in a small pan for 1–2 minutes until fragrant. Let cool slightly.
Grind the masala: Blend the roasted spices with the soaked dried chillies and coconut, adding 2–3 tbsp water, into a smooth, thick paste.
Start the curry: Heat the oil in a pan on medium heat. Add cumin seeds and let them sizzle.
Cook onion: Add the onion and cook until golden, about 4–5 minutes.
Add aromatics: Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Fry the masala paste: Add the ground Kolhapuri masala paste and cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring often, until the raw smell disappears and the oil begins to separate.
Add tomatoes: Add the tomatoes and turmeric, cooking until soft and the oil separates again, 5–6 minutes.
Add vegetables: Add the potato, carrot, beans, and cauliflower, along with enough water to just cover. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer for 12–15 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Add paneer: Stir in the peas, paneer (if using), and salt in the last 3–4 minutes, and simmer gently.
Finish: Stir in the fresh coriander before serving.

nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested.
egg_check_notes: Fully egg-free.
common_mistakes: Skipping the dry-roasting of whole spices before grinding loses a lot of depth in the final flavour. Adding too much water while grinding the masala paste makes it hard to fry off properly — keep the paste thick.
uk_sourcing_notes: Dried Kashmiri and regular dried red chillies are available at Indian grocers, and sometimes in the world foods aisle of larger Tesco/Sainsbury's stores. Kashmiri chillies are mainly for colour with mild heat — don't substitute all of them with hot dried chillies, or the dish becomes extremely fiery.
storage_notes: The curry keeps 2 days refrigerated and improves overnight. It freezes well without the paneer — add fresh paneer when reheating.
kid_friendly_notes: This dish is traditionally very spicy — reduce the number of regular dried red chillies substantially (keeping mostly the milder Kashmiri ones for colour) for a kid-friendly version.
